title: Sly, subversive and surprisingly modern: why Agatha Christie is still making a killing
summary:
A century after her mysterious 11-day disappearance, the Queen of Crime is everywhere. With an exhibition at the British Library, a new Miss Marple novel and a hot young Poirot hitting the screen, how did the novelist become such big business?

On the evening of 4 December 1926, Teresa Neele checked into the Swan Hydropathic hotel in Harrogate. A tall, attractive woman in her mid-30s with reddish hair and grey eyes, she had travelled from South Africa and carried just cash, a comb, a hot-water bottle and a photograph of a boy, the name Teddy written on the back. At dinner she told a guest that her daughter had died, and later danced the Charleston – “not very well”, according to those who were there.

Neele spent the next 10 days shopping, going to the library, playing billiards and visiting the thermal baths. She placed an ad in the Times: “Friends and relatives of Teresa Neele, late of South Africa, please communicate. Write Box R 702.” And then, on 14 December, journalists and police poured into the hotel with news. She wasn’t Teresa Neele – she was Agatha Christie the crime writer, missing for 11 days from her Surrey home.

The events of the past week tell instead a story of legal immunity and indeed impunity – revealing how Trump is putting himself, the tech bros and even artificial intelligence above the law.

It can be hard to see that through the thicket of questions that surround this episode, each one of which, don’t get me wrong, merits attention. Consider the personal profit Trump made thanks to his re-installation of Huang as the CEO of Nvidia, the world’s leading maker of advanced AI chips. Breaking the norm observed by previous presidents who, keen to avoid even the appearance of a conflict of interest, either divested themselves of stock holdings or placed them in a blind trust, Trump cheerfully buys and sells stocks in companies whose fates he can influence. He saw the value of his shares in Nvidia plunge when Huang was forced out, following revelations that the CEO had had an affair with Alice Huang, reportedly an asset of Chinese intelligence. Last weekend Trump urged the board to reconsider; Huang was reinstated on Monday and Nvidia’s value promptly soared – putting $15m in Trump’s pocket. Not for the first time, he had used the power of his office to enrich himself.

So how did “till the cows come home” come to mean never? Stranger still, when the phrase first appears in a 1587 commentary on St Paul’s epistle to the Galatians, there is only one cow. By the time playwrights Beaumont and Fletcher take it up a few decades later, their characters are kissing and drinking till the cow – still single – comes home. What began as a promise of endless pleasure has become a sigh of futility.

Jeremy Butterfield’s Metaphor Zoo is full of such linguistic metamorphoses. Butterfield is a lexicographer by trade, the man the OUP entrusted with revising Fowler’s Modern English Usage. His guiding text is Lakoff and Johnson’s Metaphors We Live By (1980), which argues that metaphors don’t just colour how we speak but structure our thinking. In this sprightly but well-grounded book (metaphor alert), Butterfield asks what mental patterns lie behind the hundreds of animal phrases in English. Then in Johnsonian fashion, he sets about tracing the original, dating each through the Oxford English Dictionary and watching as it goes walkabout.

I also knew I’d need to get to grips with the somewhat tricky aiming and shooting if I was to commit any sort of respectable crime spree.

But for the first few hours of playing this staggeringly large and bewildering game, what concerned me most was lead character Jason’s personal routine. Each day, he needs to get up, choose an outfit, complete a workout, feed his pet snake Dolores, and perhaps do some DIY, so that when his girlfriend Lucia gets out of jail she’ll fall for him again – rather than fall through his apartment’s rotten staircase. Meanwhile, his drug-smuggling boss phones every five minutes with new parcels for Jason to pick up or drop off, and his pals Cal and Donnie get into all sorts of cocaine-related hijinks they expect Jason to extricate them from. There are also predatory neighbours to do favours for, and groceries to buy. I’ve seen so many people on social media posting about how they took several days off work to play this game, only to find themselves busier and more productive than ever.
